statement: If two medial areas incommensurable with one another be added together, the remaining two irrational straight lines arise, namely either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas.
heath_proof: For let two medial areas AB, CD incommensurable with one another be added together; I say that the “side” of the area AD is either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas. For AB is either greater or less than CD. First, if it so chance, let AB be greater than CD. Let the rational straight line EF be set out, and to EF let there be applied the rectangle EG equal to AB and producing EH as breadth, and the rectangle HI equal to CD and producing HK as breadth. Now, since each of the areas AB, CD is medial, therefore each of the areas EG, HI is also medial. And they are applied to the rational straight line FE, producing EH, HK as breadth; therefore each of the straight lines EH, HK is rational and incommensurable in length with EF. [X. 22] And, since AB is incommensurable with CD, and AB is equal to EG, and CD to HI, therefore EG is also incommensurable with HI. But, as EG is to HI, so is EH to HK; [VI. 1] therefore EH is incommensurable in length with HK. [X. 11] Therefore EH, HK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore EK is binomial. [X. 36] But the square on EH is greater than the square on HK either by the square on a straight line commensurable with EH or by the square on a straight line incommensurable with it. First, let the square on it be greater by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with itself. Now neither of the straight lines EH, HK is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out; therefore EK is a third binomial. [X. Deff. II. 3] But EF is rational; and, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the third binomial, the “side” of the area is a second bimedial; [X. 56] therefore the “side” of EI, that is, of AD, is a second bimedial. Next, let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with EH. Now each of the straight lines EH, HK is incommensurable in length with EF; therefore EK is a sixth binomial. [X. Deff. II. 6] But, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the sixth binomial, the “side” of the area is the side of the sum of two medial areas; [X. 59] so that the “side” of the area AD is also the side of the sum of two medial areas.

10.72
**Statement:** If two medial areas incommensurable with one another be added together, the remaining two irrational straight lines arise, namely either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 1.** Let AB and CD be two medial areas incommensurable with one another, and let their sum be equal to the area EF. We are to show that the straight line equal in square to EF is either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line G, and to G let there be applied a rectangle EH equal to AB, producing EK as breadth, and a rectangle HF equal to CD, producing HK as breadth, so that EF = EH + HF is applied to G with total breadth EK + HK. [By 1.44 and 1.45, any rectilineal area can be applied as a rectangle to a given straight line.]

**Step 3.** Since AB is a medial area and AB = EH = G times EK, and G is rational, by 10.22 the breadth EK is rational and incommensurable in length with G. Similarly, since CD is medial and CD = HF = G times HK, by 10.22 the breadth HK is rational and incommensurable in length with G.

**Step 4.** Since AB and CD are incommensurable with one another, EH is incommensurable with HF. But EH = G times EK and HF = G times HK. Since EH is incommensurable with HF, and these rectangles share the common side G, by 6.1 (rectangles under the same height are as their bases), EK is to HK as EH is to HF. Therefore EK is incommensurable with HK [by 10.11, since EH is incommensurable with HF].

**Step 5.** Now EK and HK are both rational (Step 3) and incommensurable in length with one another (Step 4). Therefore EK and HK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [since rational straight lines incommensurable in length are commensurable in square by D10.1.3].

**Step 6.** By 10.36, since EK and HK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the whole EK + HK is a binomial straight line.

**Step 7.** Since EF is applied to the rational straight line G, and EF equals the rectangle contained by G and (EK + HK), the side of the square equal to EF is determined by the nature of the binomial EK + HK applied to the rational line G. Now EK + HK is a binomial. By the classification of binomials (D10.2.1 through D10.2.6), EK + HK is one of the six binomial types.

**Step 8.** We now determine which types of binomial EK + HK can be. Both EK and HK are incommensurable in length with G (Step 3). By the definitions of the six binomial types: a first binomial requires the greater term to be commensurable in length with the rational line set out (D10.2.1); a second binomial requires the lesser term to be commensurable in length with the rational line (D10.2.2); a fourth binomial requires the greater term to be commensurable in length with the rational line (D10.2.4); and a fifth binomial requires the lesser term to be commensurable in length with the rational line (D10.2.5). Since neither EK nor HK is commensurable in length with G, the binomial EK + HK cannot be a first, second, fourth, or fifth binomial.

**Step 9.** Therefore EK + HK is either a third binomial (D10.2.3) or a sixth binomial (D10.2.6), since these are the types where neither term is commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out.

**Step 10.** Case I: If EK + HK is a third binomial. Then by 10.56, the side of the area EF (which equals the rectangle contained by the rational straight line G and the third binomial EK + HK) is a second bimedial straight line.

**Step 11.** Case II: If EK + HK is a sixth binomial. Then by 10.59, the side of the area EF (which equals the rectangle contained by the rational straight line G and the sixth binomial EK + HK) is the side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 12.** Therefore, when two medial areas incommensurable with one another are added together, the straight line equal in square to their sum is either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas. No other irrational type arises, since the binomial formed by the breadths must be either third or sixth, and these correspond precisely to the second bimedial and the side of the sum of two medial areas respectively. Q.E.D.
